```text
1	\section{Discussion}
2	\label{sec:discussion}
3	
4	\paragraph{Depth-graduated curation and deployment.}
5	Predicted depth can serve as a quality proxy for importance weighting \cite{dsir2023,qurating2024}, down-weighting deeply recursive samples that binary filters \cite{drayson2025_detection_prevents_collapse} would indiscriminately discard.
6	However, cross-strategy deployment faces a significant obstacle: the temperature-induced d1/d2 boundary inversion (GPT-2~XL d1v2 AUC$\,{=}\,$0.129, OLMo$\,{=}\,$0.253; \S\ref{sec:gen:crossstrategy}) means that a classifier trained without knowledge of the decoding strategy may systematically misrank depths.
7	Per-strategy normalization partially corrects the scale component but leaves a residual gap that simple feature normalization cannot resolve; whether more sophisticated domain adaptation methods could recover the boundary remains open.
8	Reliable cross-strategy deployment therefore requires a two-stage pipeline---automatic strategy identification followed by strategy-conditioned classification---making strategy detection a prerequisite rather than an optional enhancement.
9	
10	\paragraph{Mixed-depth corpora.}
11	Our evaluation assumes each passage is generated at a single depth, yet real-world documents may interleave human-written and machine-generated segments at different recursion depths within the same text.
12	Passage-level classification would assign a single depth label to such mixed documents, potentially producing misleading estimates.
13	Extending the framework to segment-level depth estimation---detecting depth transitions within a document---is a natural next step, though it introduces additional challenges in boundary detection and short-segment feature reliability.
14	
15	\paragraph{Adversarial robustness.}
16	Adversarial paraphrasing and post-hoc editing could disrupt the statistical fingerprints that our method relies on, particularly the perplexity tail features.
17	\citet{sadasivan2023_paraphrase} demonstrate that paraphrasing attacks reduce binary detection accuracy to near chance; similar attacks would likely degrade depth estimation.
18	Depth estimation and watermarking \cite{kirchenbauer2023_watermark} address complementary aspects of provenance---the former operates retroactively on any text, while the latter requires proactive embedding---and combining both could provide more robust provenance tracking.
19	
20	\paragraph{Data provenance.}
21	Depth estimation contributes one dimension to a broader data provenance toolkit.
22	Combined with model attribution \cite{uchendu2020_attribution} (identifying \emph{which} model generated a text) and watermarking (verifying \emph{whether} a specific model generated it), depth estimation answers a distinct question: \emph{how many recursive iterations} has the text undergone.
23	These complementary signals could be integrated into a unified provenance pipeline for training data auditing.
24	
25	\paragraph{Scaling to larger models and deeper recursion.}
26	Our benchmark covers 1--1.5B parameter models at depths up to $d{=}5$.
27	Larger models (7B--70B+) may exhibit different collapse dynamics---potentially slower degradation due to greater capacity, or altered feature hierarchies---and deeper recursion ($d > 5$) may reveal new regimes beyond the signal saturation observed at $d{=}5$.
28	Extending the benchmark to these scales will require addressing computational costs of multi-generation pipelines and may necessitate more efficient feature computation than full reference-model inference.
29	
```

```text
1	\section{Discussion}
2	\label{sec:discussion}
3	
4	\paragraph{Depth-graduated curation and deployment.}
5	Predicted depth can serve as a quality proxy for importance weighting \cite{dsir2023,qurating2024}, down-weighting deeply recursive samples that binary filters \cite{drayson2025_detection_prevents_collapse} would indiscriminately discard.
6	However, cross-strategy deployment faces a significant obstacle: the temperature-induced d1/d2 boundary inversion (GPT-2~XL d1v2 AUC$\,{=}\,$0.129, OLMo$\,{=}\,$0.253; \S\ref{sec:gen:crossstrategy}) means that a classifier trained without knowledge of the decoding strategy may systematically misrank depths.
7	Per-strategy normalization partially corrects the scale component but leaves a residual gap that simple feature normalization cannot resolve; whether more sophisticated domain adaptation methods could recover the boundary remains open.
8	Reliable cross-strategy deployment therefore requires a two-stage pipeline---automatic strategy identification followed by strategy-conditioned classification---making strategy detection a prerequisite rather than an optional enhancement.
9	
10	\paragraph{Mixed-depth corpora.}
11	Our evaluation assumes each passage is generated at a single depth, yet real-world documents may interleave human-written and machine-generated segments at different recursion depths within the same text.
12	Passage-level classification would assign a single depth label to such mixed documents, potentially producing misleading estimates.
13	Extending the framework to segment-level depth estimation---detecting depth transitions within a document---is a natural next step, though it introduces additional challenges in boundary detection and short-segment feature reliability.
14	
15	\paragraph{Adversarial robustness.}
16	Adversarial paraphrasing and post-hoc editing could disrupt the statistical fingerprints that our method relies on, particularly the perplexity tail features.
17	\citet{sadasivan2023_paraphrase} demonstrate that paraphrasing attacks reduce binary detection accuracy to near chance; similar attacks would likely degrade depth estimation.
18	Depth estimation and watermarking \cite{kirchenbauer2023_watermark} address complementary aspects of provenance---the former operates retroactively on any text, while the latter requires proactive embedding---and combining both could provide more robust provenance tracking.
19	
20	\paragraph{Data provenance.}
21	Depth estimation contributes one dimension to a broader data provenance toolkit.
22	Combined with model attribution \cite{uchendu2020_attribution} (identifying \emph{which} model generated a text) and watermarking (verifying \emph{whether} a specific model generated it), depth estimation answers a distinct question: \emph{how many recursive iterations} has the text undergone.
23	These complementary signals could be integrated into a unified provenance pipeline for training data auditing.
24	
25	\paragraph{Scaling to larger models and deeper recursion.}
26	Our benchmark covers 1--1.5B parameter models at depths up to $d{=}5$.
27	Larger models (7B--70B+) may exhibit different collapse dynamics---potentially slower degradation due to greater capacity, or altered feature hierarchies---and deeper recursion ($d > 5$) may reveal new regimes beyond the signal saturation observed at $d{=}5$.
28	Extending the benchmark to these scales will require addressing computational costs of multi-generation pipelines and may necessitate more efficient feature computation than full reference-model inference.
29	
```

    "oldString": "\\paragraph{Depth-graduated curation and deployment.}\nPredicted depth can serve as a quality proxy for importance weighting \\cite{dsir2023,qurating2024}, down-weighting deeply recursive samples that binary filters \\cite{drayson2025_detection_prevents_collapse} would indiscriminately discard.\nHowever, cross-strategy deployment faces a significant obstacle: the temperature-induced d1/d2 boundary inversion (GPT-2~XL d1v2 AUC$\\,{=}\\,$0.129, OLMo$\\,{=}\\,$0.253; \\S\\ref{sec:gen:crossstrategy}) means that a classifier trained without knowledge of the decoding strategy may systematically misrank depths.\nPer-strategy normalization partially corrects the scale component but leaves a residual gap that simple feature normalization cannot resolve; whether more sophisticated domain adaptation methods could recover the boundary remains open.\nReliable cross-strategy deployment therefore requires a two-stage pipeline---automatic strategy identification followed by strategy-conditioned classification---making strategy detection a prerequisite rather than an optional enhancement.\n\n\\paragraph{Mixed-depth corpora.}\nOur evaluation assumes each passage is generated at a single depth, yet real-world documents may interleave human-written and machine-generated segments at different recursion depths within the same text.\nPassage-level classification would assign a single depth label to such mixed documents, potentially producing misleading estimates.\nExtending the framework to segment-level depth estimation---detecting depth transitions within a document---is a natural next step, though it introduces additional challenges in boundary detection and short-segment feature reliability.\n\n\\paragraph{Adversarial robustness.}\nAdversarial paraphrasing and post-hoc editing could disrupt the statistical fingerprints that our method relies on, particularly the perplexity tail features.\n\\citet{sadasivan2023_paraphrase} demonstrate that paraphrasing attacks reduce binary detection accuracy to near chance; similar attacks would likely degrade depth estimation.\nDepth estimation and watermarking \\cite{kirchenbauer2023_watermark} address complementary aspects of provenance---the former operates retroactively on any text, while the latter requires proactive embedding---and combining both could provide more robust provenance tracking.\n\n\\paragraph{Data provenance.}\nDepth estimation contributes one dimension to a broader data provenance toolkit.\nCombined with model attribution \\cite{uchendu2020_attribution} (identifying \\emph{which} model generated a text) and watermarking (verifying \\emph{whether} a specific model generated it), depth estimation answers a distinct question: \\emph{how many recursive iterations} has the text undergone.\nThese complementary signals could be integrated into a unified provenance pipeline for training data auditing.\n\n\\paragraph{Scaling to larger models and deeper recursion.}\nOur benchmark covers 1--1.5B parameter models at depths up to $d{=}5$.\nLarger models (7B--70B+) may exhibit different collapse dynamics---potentially slower degradation due to greater capacity, or altered feature hierarchies---and deeper recursion ($d > 5$) may reveal new regimes beyond the signal saturation observed at $d{=}5$.\nExtending the benchmark to these scales will require addressing computational costs of multi-generation pipelines and may necessitate more efficient feature computation than full reference-model inference.",

    "originalFile": "\\section{Discussion}\n\\label{sec:discussion}\n\n\\paragraph{Depth-graduated curation and deployment.}\nPredicted depth can serve as a quality proxy for importance weighting \\cite{dsir2023,qurating2024}, down-weighting deeply recursive samples that binary filters \\cite{drayson2025_detection_prevents_collapse} would indiscriminately discard.\nHowever, cross-strategy deployment faces a significant obstacle: the temperature-induced d1/d2 boundary inversion (GPT-2~XL d1v2 AUC$\\,{=}\\,$0.129, OLMo$\\,{=}\\,$0.253; \\S\\ref{sec:gen:crossstrategy}) means that a classifier trained without knowledge of the decoding strategy may systematically misrank depths.\nPer-strategy normalization partially corrects the scale component but leaves a residual gap that simple feature normalization cannot resolve; whether more sophisticated domain adaptation methods could recover the boundary remains open.\nReliable cross-strategy deployment therefore requires a two-stage pipeline---automatic strategy identification followed by strategy-conditioned classification---making strategy detection a prerequisite rather than an optional enhancement.\n\n\\paragraph{Mixed-depth corpora.}\nOur evaluation assumes each passage is generated at a single depth, yet real-world documents may interleave human-written and machine-generated segments at different recursion depths within the same text.\nPassage-level classification would assign a single depth label to such mixed documents, potentially producing misleading estimates.\nExtending the framework to segment-level depth estimation---detecting depth transitions within a document---is a natural next step, though it introduces additional challenges in boundary detection and short-segment feature reliability.\n\n\\paragraph{Adversarial robustness.}\nAdversarial paraphrasing and post-hoc editing could disrupt the statistical fingerprints that our method relies on, particularly the perplexity tail features.\n\\citet{sadasivan2023_paraphrase} demonstrate that paraphrasing attacks reduce binary detection accuracy to near chance; similar attacks would likely degrade depth estimation.\nDepth estimation and watermarking \\cite{kirchenbauer2023_watermark} address complementary aspects of provenance---the former operates retroactively on any text, while the latter requires proactive embedding---and combining both could provide more robust provenance tracking.\n\n\\paragraph{Data provenance.}\nDepth estimation contributes one dimension to a broader data provenance toolkit.\nCombined with model attribution \\cite{uchendu2020_attribution} (identifying \\emph{which} model generated a text) and watermarking (verifying \\emph{whether} a specific model generated it), depth estimation answers a distinct question: \\emph{how many recursive iterations} has the text undergone.\nThese complementary signals could be integrated into a unified provenance pipeline for training data auditing.\n\n\\paragraph{Scaling to larger models and deeper recursion.}\nOur benchmark covers 1--1.5B parameter models at depths up to $d{=}5$.\nLarger models (7B--70B+) may exhibit different collapse dynamics---potentially slower degradation due to greater capacity, or altered feature hierarchies---and deeper recursion ($d > 5$) may reveal new regimes beyond the signal saturation observed at $d{=}5$.\nExtending the benchmark to these scales will require addressing computational costs of multi-generation pipelines and may necessitate more efficient feature computation than full reference-model inference.\n",
